title: fix(bin): recognize antigravity acp as agy and stop parking its Stop hook
body:
## Intent Recognize T3 Code's bundled Antigravity ACP server (antigravity acp) as the agy harness for detection and session locking, align fm-harness.sh ancestry walk depth with fm-session-lock-lib.sh (16 hops) so deep SessionStart hook chains do not fall back to inherited CLAUDECODE, and avoid synchronous Stop-hook parking under antigravity acp because ACP awaits Stop before completing the turn and blocks incoming user messages. ## What Changed - New `bin/fm-agy-process-lib.sh` matches both the standalone `agy` CLI and T3 Code's bundled `antigravity acp` server, using anchored rules so Electron `Antigravity` processes and plain `antigravity` runs without `acp` don't match. `fm-harness.sh` and `fm-session-lock-lib.sh` now both use it, so an ACP session is detected as `agy` and can take the session lock. - `fm-harness.sh` now walks 16 parent hops instead of 8, in both `harness_ancestry` and `ancestry_names_omp`, which matches `fm-session-lock-lib.sh`. Deep SessionStart hook chains now reach the owning harness process instead of falling back to an inherited `CLAUDECODE` marker. - Under `antigravity acp`, `fm-turnend-guard-agy.sh` hands off right away to the non-parking `fm-turnend-guard.sh --agy` backstop instead of parking on Stop, and `fm_supervision_model` reports `persistent` instead of `autoarm`. `fm-supervision-instructions.sh` renders the new `docs/supervision-protocols/agy-acp.md` protocol, which arms the watcher as a background `run_command` task, and it gives ACP its own repair and ordinary-wake lines. The agy, turn-end guard, supervision host and verification docs plus tests are updated to match. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: The change does what the intent asks. One shared matcher detects antigravity acp. Both ancestry walks in fm-harness.sh now go 16 hops. Under ACP, the Stop hook hands off to the non-parking bounded guard, and the persistent model and background-arm instructions come from the same ancestry check. Tracing the callers, tag rendering, and the round-2 consolidation found no wrong-result path, and only owning-doc staleness remains. ## Testing Every live run used the machine's real Antigravity binary. Each ran against a throwaway primary checkout in a marked `bin/fm-lab-home.sh` lab, built from `git archive` of HEAD or of the base commit. Antigravity ACP was driven over stdio by a small JSON-RPC client. The full session transcript and the tool outputs reported by the server were captured as evidence. Fixed ACP sessions detect as agy with CLAUDECODE=1 inherited, at shallow depth and with 12 extra nested hops. They lock the antigravity pid, report the `persistent` supervision model and select `agy-acp.md` plus the background-arm supervision-host lines. Their Stop hook nags instead of parking. Turns completed in 9 to 43s, and a follow-up prompt was answered while the background `fm-watch-arm.sh` the model armed kept running. The base commit misdetects the same process as claude and locks a foreign `claude` pid. Removing only the new non-park branch makes the Stop hook park `fm-watch-arm.sh` and leaves turns unanswered for more than 200s. Standalone `agy` (the same binary exec'd under the `agy` name) still parks on Stop. The four targeted test files pass. Non-ACP lookalike shapes were covered only by fixture-based tests, not live. I killed every watcher process started during the runs by its recorded PID and removed all lab homes. The worktree is clean. The change has no visual UI, so the evidence is ACP transcripts and process samples rather than screenshots. - Live validation: ✅ go - 8 of 9 scenarios driven live against the product | Scenario | Result | Live | Evidence | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A real T3 Code `antigravity acp` session with CLAUDECODE=1 inherited runs bin/fm-harness.sh via run_command and gets `agy`, and fm_supervision_model reports `persistent` | ✅ pass | live | s1-acp-readable.txt: PROBE fm-harness.sh (shallow): agy; PROBE CLAUDECODE=1; fm_supervision_model: persistent | | Deep call chain: fm-harness.sh run 12 extra nested bash hops below the real ACP server (more than the old 8-hop walk) still resolves to agy instead of falling back to the inherited CLAUDECODE | ✅ pass | live | s1-acp-readable.txt: PROBE fm-harness.sh (+12 nested bash hops, CLAUDECODE=1 inherited): agy | | ACP session open: the SessionStart hook in .agents/hooks.json takes state/.lock for the antigravity acp pid and injects the ACP background-notify protocol | ✅ pass | live | s1-acp-driver.log ACP_SERVER_PID=11709 and probe state/.lock: 11709; model quoted 'Mode: Antigravity ACP background-notify supervision.' from its session-start context | | Under ACP with an unguarded in-flight task, the Stop hook does not park. title: When two secondmate homes hold the same captain question, the relayed answer closes it in only one of them
body:
## Observed

A secondmate home records a question for the captain as a held task in its own backlog, through `bin/fm-captain-hold.sh hold`.
Two secondmate homes can each hold the same question, for example when one deferred question gates work in both homes.
Each home's hold has its own task id and decision key, and no record links the two.

The main session relays the captain's answer with `bin/fm-send.sh`, which takes one `<target>` (usage, line 4 on `427056c4`).
Its `--resolve-key` closes keys on that target only, and the pending-reply record for the message names that one target.
So the first home records the answer, its relay record reaches `resolved`, and the main home shows the answer as delivered.
The second home's hold stays open, and no record in the main home shows that a second delivery is still owed.

## Expected

When the captain answers a question that more than one home holds, each holding home records the answer, or the main home keeps showing the answer as undelivered to the homes that have not recorded it.

## Consequence

In one fleet, two secondmate homes held the same deferred question.
The answer was relayed to the first home only.
That home recorded it, wrote that it could not close the other home's copy, and asked for the answer to be routed there.
The second home reported 16 hours 44 minutes after the relay that the answer had reached only the first home.

## How to verify a fix

1. Run two secondmate homes, and in each one hold the same captain question with `bin/fm-captain-hold.sh hold`.
2. Relay the captain's answer to one home with `bin/fm-send.sh <home> --resolve-key <key> <answer>`.
3. Check that the second home's hold is closed too, or that the main home still reports the answer as undelivered to the second home.

Related, none of which links one answer to holds in two homes:

- https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/pull/8093 (open) tells firstmate to send an answer to the one home that owns the work.
- https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/pull/8393 and https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/pull/7370 (open) let several origins share one hold inside a single home.
- https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/issues/8686 covers two records of one call inside a single home.

title: Feature request: let a ship task on the firstmate repository declare which repository it expects to publish to
body:
## Observed

For a ship task on the firstmate repository, `fm_role_gate_self_publish` (`bin/fm-role-lib.sh` lines 500-544 on `427056c4`) authorizes publication to the target that `fm_role_publication_target` (lines 230-249) resolves from the project's git remotes.
That is the first remote marked `gh-resolved=base`, otherwise the first of `upstream`, `github` and `origin`.

A task has no way to state which repository it expects to publish to.
`--upstream-consent <host>/<owner>/<repo>` is checked first, but a consent that does not match the resolved target does not refuse the task.
The gate falls through to the home's `config/firstmate-role`, and a `maintainer` grant for the resolved target authorizes the task.
So in a home with a maintainer grant for the upstream, a task meant for a fork is authorized to publish upstream whenever its project resolves to the upstream.

## Expected

A task can carry the repository it expects to publish to, and dispatch refuses the task when the resolved target is a different repository.
A task that declares nothing behaves as today.

## Consequence

In one fleet, a home held a maintainer grant for the upstream and also kept a fork that must receive changes first.
A ship task whose instructions said to land on the fork and open nothing upstream was dispatched on the project whose clone resolves to the upstream.
Its validation run targeted the upstream.
The worker noticed at its review gate and stopped before any push, so nothing was published.
The task was re-dispatched on a copy that pushes to the fork, 2 hours 6 minutes after the first dispatch.

The gate worked as designed: the home's grant covers the upstream.
The mismatch was between the destination the task stated in prose and the target that dispatch resolved, which no check compares.

## How to verify

1. In a home whose `config/firstmate-role` holds `maintainer github.com/<owner>/firstmate`, prepare a ship task on a project whose clone resolves to that repository.
2. Declare a different expected target, such as a fork, on the task.
3. Check that the spawn refuses and names both repositories.
4. Check that the same spawn without a declared target behaves as today.

Related: https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/pull/4555 (open) adds a home-wide `config/fork-url` push target for homes that cannot push upstream.
It sets one target for every task in a home, so it does not cover one task whose destination differs from the home's other tasks.

title: Would a harness adapter for the Abacus AI CLI be welcome?
body:
## Question

Would you accept a verified harness adapter for Abacus AI's terminal agent (`abacusai`)? I would like to know before anyone builds it. I run Firstmate as a user, and I would start with crew workers (scouts and ships), then look at the primary seat.

## What I know so far

This comes from Abacus's own docs. I have not run the CLI yet.

- It installs from npm as `@abacus-ai/cli` and starts with the `abacusai` command: https://abacus.ai/help/abacusai-desktop/cli-installation
- The docs describe a print mode for scripts and CI, `abacusai -p "..."`, plus built-in MCP support. They say hook scripts written for Claude Code run unchanged and that `/import` brings a Claude Code setup across, including hooks: https://abacus.ai/help/abacusai-desktop/introduction
- Subagents bundled in Claude Code plugins are not used after an import (same install page).

## What I do not know

- The headless flags and exit codes (the docs point to a separate "Scripting and CI" section I could not read).
- The workspace trust prompt, how to interrupt and exit, and what a busy screen looks like.
- The flags for model and effort.

## What an adapter would need

From `.agents/skills/harness-adapters/references/common/dispatch.md`: detection, a launch template, busy state, composer behavior, lifecycle control, tmux liveness, a portable regression test, and a verification record. It also needs a credentialed live check, so someone has to hold an Abacus login.

## What I am asking

1. Are you in favor of adding an adapter for a vendor like this, or would you rather keep it out of tree?
2. If in favor, is a crew-only adapter (no primary seat) an acceptable first step?
3. Who would cover the credentialed live check?

If the answer is yes, I can run a trial through the raw launch escape hatch and post what I find here before proposing any code.

title: fix(bin): run agy primary supervision as a background arm instead of a Stop-hook park
body:
## Intent

Fix Antigravity CLI (agy) primary supervision and deep ancestry detection in Firstmate: replace blocking 28800s synchronous Stop-hook parking with a fast non-blocking 30s Stop turn-end backstop, move agy from autoarm to the persistent supervision model using Antigravity tracked background run_command (WaitMsBeforeAsync: 5000) with reactive wakeup, widen harness_ancestry() from 8 to 16 hops to match session-lock detection, update supervision docs and harness-adapter references, and update/add test coverage.

## What Changed
- Replaces Antigravity's synchronous 28800s Stop-hook park with a fast, non-blocking turn-end backstop (`bin/fm-turnend-guard-agy.sh` now delegates to `bin/fm-turnend-guard.sh --agy` under a 30s hook timeout) and moves agy onto the persistent supervision model using Antigravity tracked background `run_command` (`WaitMsBeforeAsync: 5000`) with reactive wakeup.
- Removes agy from the autoarm mappings in `bin/fm-inbox.sh`, `bin/fm-spawn.sh`, and `bin/fm-wake-lib.sh`, renders the supervision host/arm command for agy via `__FM_AGY_ARM__` in `bin/fm-supervision-instructions.sh`, and widens `harness_ancestry()` in `bin/fm-harness.sh` from 8 to 16 hops to match session-lock detection.
- Updates the agy protocol and related supervision docs/harness-adapter references, adds first-session-start clearing of the shared `state/.turnend-blocks` budget in `bin/fm-sessionstart-agy.sh`, and rewrites the agy primary, live e2e, harness, and supervision-instruction tests for the new model.

## Risk Assessment

⚠️ Medium: The supervision redesign is coherent and materially simpler, and the new regression test exercises the stale-budget fix through real scripts, but the core tracked background run_command arm with reactive wakeup is covered only by interactive observation as the updated verification record itself states, so the highest-risk path has no automated e2e.

## Testing

Ran the agy supervision behavior suites and drove the real Stop-hook guard and session-start adapter directly in a throwaway lab home: the hook now returns fast JSON ({} or a bounded 'decision: continue' nag), never parks or writes a park-owner marker, charges at most 3 blocks then fails open, and a fresh agy session clears an exhausted block budget so its first missing-supervision turn nags. Also drove bin/fm-harness.sh against a real nested process tree: agy is now detected 14 hops up but not beyond the 16-hop bound. The only scenario I could not drive live is the real agy CLI: its login cannot be reproduced in an isolated HOME (every file-copy attempt still prompted for OAuth, and using the real HOME would require signing in or trusting a disposable workspace in user-level agy config, both forbidden), so the tracked-background run_command arm plus reactive wakeup remain unproven here beyond the recorded interactive observation.

- ℹ️ `bin/fm-harness.sh:338` - The `process_descent_path` comment still says it is "Bounded to the same eight levels harness_ancestry climbs", but `harness_ancestry` now climbs 16 hops (bin/fm-harness.sh:318), so the stated parity invariant is false and could mislead a future reader into thinking the two walks are matched. The Stop-continuation loop is already bounded by the shared guard's `state/.turnend-blocks` budget (fm-turnend-guard.sh:block_stop), so this branch is not needed for loop safety. Please confirm the field's agy provenance/semantics (and record it in the verification record) or drop the early stand-down.
- ⚠️ `tests/fm-agy-primary-live-e2e.test.sh:98` - This change removes the only live evidence that agy supervision delivers a wake (the old Stop-park e2e) and replaces it with a guard-only check that runs agy via `-p` one-shot. Nothing now exercises the new core mechanism - tracked background `run_command` arm plus reactive wakeup - even though docs/supervision-protocols/agy.md:24 makes it the entire continuity path and docs/verification/agy.md:162 states it as an established fact in a record that owns "what is still unproven". Either point to the evidence that this vendor behavior was observed (interactive TUI; note grok's documented `-p` limitation) and record it, or add this to docs/verification/agy.md "What is still unproven" so the admitted gap is not presented as proven.
- ⚠️ `bin/fm-supervision-instructions.sh:125` - Simplification: `agy_arm` is a second, parallel definition of the exact rule `grok_arm` already encodes (both default to `bin/fm-watch-arm.sh` and both become `bin/fm-supervision-host.sh park` under the same `fm_supervision_host_enabled` gate at lines 131-134), requiring a duplicated substitution at line 197 and duplicated assignments at 133. The intent needs an agy arm command, not a duplicated variable. One shared arm-command variable (used for both placeholders) satisfies the same requirement with one definition; remove the duplicate.

🔧 Fix applied.
1 warning still open:

- ⚠️ `docs/verification/agy.md:163` - Residual of the fix round that addressed F4: the record now says the tracked background `run_command` arm and its reactive wakeup "were observed interactively in the `agy` TUI", but omits the agy version and date the observation was made on (the fix instructions named `agy 1.5.15`). This record owns "how they were established", and its own Subject table (docs/verification/agy.md:10) still states `Version | agy 1.2.0`, `Verified | 2026-09-10`, so the new claim about a version-dependent tool schema (`WaitMsBeforeAsync`, `IsDaemon`) contradicts the record's stated subject. Align the changed claim with the evidence: name the observed version/date here, and note it in the Subject table (or mark that row as covering only the pre-background findings). Sibling site that must stay consistent: `.agents/skills/harness-adapters/references/harness/agy.md:3` still describes the whole adapter as "verified end to end with agy 1.2.0+" while its changed lines 58-59 now assert the background-arm behavior as an operating fact.

🔧 Fix applied.
3 issues (2 warnings, 1 info) still open:

- ⚠️ `tests/fm-agy-primary-live-e2e.test.sh:113` - The second half of the new non-blocking Stop-hook check cannot fail when the guard is wrong. The prompt only asks the model to reply CLEAN_EXIT, and a model receiving an erroneous `TURN WOULD END BLIND` nag (block_stop returns `decision: continue`) still eventually prints CLEAN_EXIT in some turn, so this assertion passes even if an empty fleet wrongly triggers up to three repair blocks. That contradicts the claimed behavior "the Stop hook allows clean exit" and the section comment at line 100-101. Reject a wrong implementation by also asserting the run produced no nag and charged no block budget, e.g. `assert_not_contains "$OUT" "TURN WOULD END BLIND"` plus `[ ! -e "$HOME_DIR/state/.turnend-blocks" ]` after the clean run. (The first half, GUARD_FIRED plus the absent `.agy-park-owner`, is discriminating and can stay.)
- ⚠️ `README.md:80` - The user-facing primary-harness summary is now false: it says Antigravity uses an `.agents/hooks.json` "whose Stop hook parks on the watcher between turns like Cursor's", but this change removes that park (`.agents/hooks.json` Stop is now a 30s non-blocking backstop and supervision is the model's tracked background `run_command`, as documented in docs/turnend-guard.md:556-567 and docs/supervision-protocols/agy.md:1-34). This is the only remaining doc outside the changed set that still describes the removed park; `docs/turnend-guard.md`, `docs/supervision-host.md`, `docs/supervision-protocols/*`, and `.agents/skills/harness-adapters/references/harness/agy.md` were all updated. Update the sentence to describe the tracked background arm plus the 30s backstop.
- ℹ️ `bin/fm-supervision-instructions.sh:10` - Stale source comment after the arm-variable unification: the header still says only "Grok's arm command becomes the host", but this change makes Antigravity an arm owner of the supervision host too (`{grok,agy}` in docs/supervision-protocols/supervision-host.md, `persistent_arm` substituted for both `__FM_GROK_ARM__` and `__FM_AGY_ARM__`). Sibling with the same drift: bin/fm-supervision-host.sh:12-18 lists every host arm owner except agy (Grok's model-owned background arm is named, Antigravity's is not). Mechanical comment correction only; behavior is correct.

🔧 Fix applied.
1 warning still open:

- ⚠️ `bin/fm-turnend-guard-agy.sh:56` - The new non-blocking backstop delegates to `bin/fm-turnend-guard.sh --agy`, whose only supervision-repair signal is the `.turnend-blocks` counter, and that counter is not session-scoped (unlike Claude's session-keyed `BUDGET_FILE`). Concrete sequence: session A has in-flight tasks and no healthy watcher; the guard nags 3 times, `.turnend-blocks` = 3, and the captain quits before the model re-arms. Session B starts on the same home with tasks still in flight; the model does not arm on its first cycle (exactly the failure the backstop exists to catch). At the first Stop, `bin/fm-turnend-guard.sh:276-281` reads 3, `cur_blocks >= max_blocks`, prints `{}` and exits, so session B gets no `TURN WOULD END BLIND` nag and supervision stays off silently until something makes the watcher healthy or empties the fleet. `bin/fm-sessionstart-agy.sh` (and `bin/fm-sessionstart-run.sh`) never clear the counter, and this change removed the old wrapper's own bounded arm attempts plus `FM_AGY_TURNEND_LOOP_CEILING`, so nothing else restores supervision once the inherited budget is exhausted. The same invariant ('a new agy session's first missing-supervision turn must produce its bounded repair nag') must also hold at the shared budget owner `bin/fm-turnend-guard.sh:273-284` and at session open in `bin/fm-sessionstart-agy.sh`. Smallest honest remedy: clear `state/.turnend-blocks` at agy session start (or record the payload sessionId beside the count and reset on change), keeping the 3-block bound per session.

🔧 Fix applied.
✅ Re-checked - no issues remain.

title: fix(watch): absorb turn-end wakes after a user-aborted no-mistakes run
body:
Closes #8675 ## What Changed - Add `crew_aborted_run_superseded_by_busy` in `bin/fm-classify-lib.sh`, wired into `signal_crew_provably_working`. With `config/turnend-abort-absorb` present, a bare turn-end is absorbed when the task's current-state read is a run-step failed or unknown verdict. The named run must also be terminal in the no-mistakes run store with an explicit user-abort record. The busy-state verdict must be exactly `busy `, with a record timestamp newer than the run's last update. The flag is default-off, and any other shape surfaces as before. - Document the flag in `docs/configuration.md` ("Aborted-run turn-end absorb"), `docs/architecture.md` and the operational-home-layout skill. - Add watch-triage tests for the new absorb path. Update `tests/fm-afk-launch.test.sh`. Rename a local variable in `bin/fm-busy-lib.sh` and quote a value in `bin/fm-home-summary-refresh.sh` to clear ShellCheck findings. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: The absorb path stays behind a default-off flag. It now takes the busy verdict from `fm_busy_classify_meta` as the maintainer asked, and it has a surfacing test row for the untrusted fm-spawn respawn seed. The lint fixes are behavior-neutral renames and one added pair of quotes. ## Testing I ran the abort-absorb test on its own. It drives the real classifier against a sqlite run record and fixture busy-state records. It passed all 17 cases: flag off, cancelled and gate-abort variants, older or equal busy timestamps, idle and unknown verdicts, a stale generation, a missing run id, an untrusted respawn-seeded fm-spawn record that must surface, and a trusted one that is absorbed. The full watch-triage file stopped at "expired stream did not enter inspection timer", a pi-stream test unrelated to this change. I did not re-run it on the base commit to confirm it also fails there. The afk-launch test, which the lint fix touched, passed everywhere except its herdr e2e case. title: feat(bin): add --since-last-ack flag to fm-wake-drain.sh
body:
## Problem

Repeated supervision wake drains reprint the full annotation history for every watched task. For long-running secondmates like weir-promo, a single drain can produce 80+ lines of historical events that the firstmate primary has already seen and acknowledged. This wastes significant context on every supervision cycle.

## Proposal

Add an opt-in `--since-last-ack` flag to `bin/fm-wake-drain.sh` that filters annotations to only those newer than the last acknowledged drain generation's epoch. The flag is backward compatible: without it, all annotations print as before.

The last-ack epoch is recorded durably when `--ack-through` successfully removes rows, and read back on the next `--since-last-ack` presentation. Lines without a parseable `[at=EPOCH]` pass through unfiltered.

Full drains (without the flag) remain appropriate for session-start, recovery, and after-return drains.

title: feat(bin): add --since-last-ack flag to fm-wake-drain.sh
body:
## Summary
Long-running supervision drains reprint every historical status annotation each time, which wastes context. This PR adds an opt-in flag to the wake drain that prints only annotations newer than the last acknowledgement, and fixes a defect in the first version where the flag's default was set after option parsing: the flag never filtered anything, and every plain acknowledgement aborted with an unbound-variable error. Both the flag and plain acknowledgements now behave as described.

## What's added
- **Wake drain.** New `--since-last-ack` flag: annotation lines stamped `[at=EPOCH]` at or before the last acknowledged wake's epoch are omitted; lines without a stamp still print. Without the flag, output is unchanged.
- **Wake drain.** Each `--ack-through` acknowledgement records the newest acknowledged wake epoch so the flag has a cutoff to read.
- **Wake drain.** `--since-last-ack` combined with `--ack-through` is refused with exit 2.
- **Docs.** The architecture notes describe the flag.

## User journey and behavior changes
- **Before:** every drain reprinted all historical annotation lines. **Now:** `bin/fm-wake-drain.sh --since-last-ack` prints only lines newer than the last acknowledgement; a plain drain is unchanged.
- **What you need to do:** nothing; the flag is opt-in.

## Testing
- Setup: Linux (WSL2), GNU bash 5.2, repository checkout run in place, temporary state directories with fake status lines.

title: fix(omp): consume every watcher wake omp merges into one message
body:
## Intent Have you notice that there are alot of wake every time I opened the session that wrong with it? Context for that question and the answer it was given: on an omp primary, every new session receives the same 77 old watcher wakes (from 16-21 Nov) as one burst right after the first `fm_watch_arm_omp`. They come from the replacement handoff `state/extensions/omp-primary-watch/session-replacement-actionable.json` written by `.omp/extensions/fm-primary-omp-watch.ts`. On replay, omp delivers the queued follow-ups merged into ONE user message with ONE text part holding all 77 wake texts (verified in the omp session log: one `message` entry, role user, 1 content part, 77 occurrences of `FIRSTMATE WATCHER WAKE`). `consumeWake` finishes a pending record only when the whole user text equals one wake's content exactly, so none of the 77 is ever finished, they stay in `pendingActionables`, and `stopSessionGeneration` persists them again at every shutdown. The oldest record has been replayed in every session since 18 Nov. Single wakes delivered to an idle main are consumed normally, which is why the set stopped growing after 21 Nov; it grows again whenever several follow-ups are merged while main is busy. Recommendation given, which was then accepted ("I will go with your recommendation."): clear the stale saved list once locally at the next session start (handled by firstmate, not this task), and fix the matching so each wake inside a merged message counts as consumed, sent upstream as a pull request from the fork. That upstream pull request is approved as this one contribution. ## What Changed - `consumeWake` in `.omp/extensions/fm-primary-omp-watch.ts` now matches by containment instead of whole-text equality. A user message or prompt that carries several queued wakes (omp merges replayed follow-ups into one text part, joined by a blank line) now finishes each pending wake it contains. Wakes are matched longest-content first. Each matched occurrence is cut out of the text, so identical wakes need as many occurrences. Text that lacks a wake's full content still consumes nothing. Each scenario asserts which wakes remain in the handoff and that no extra follow-ups are sent. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: The change is a small, well-bounded matching fix in `consumeWake`, and the new test runs the real extension against a seeded handoff with an independent oracle. title: fix(bin): carry Herdr pre-launch exports in the staged launch command
body:
## Intent

Fix Herdr launch-line fusion in bin/fm-spawn.sh: because herdr pane run returns once text is typed before zsh finishes submitting the line, sending back-to-back pre-launch export lines followed by the launch source line fuses them into one broken command (export COMPACT_ADVISER_DISABLE=1. '/tmp/fm-.../launch.s....sh') and leaves workers dead. Carry Herdr pre-launch exports at the head of the staged launch command so Herdr performs one single text write while preserving non-Herdr backends, trace-context rollback semantics, and env-allowlist invariants, with regression tests and updated docs.

## What Changed
- Route Herdr's pre-launch `export` statements (GOTMPDIR, COMPACT_ADVISER_DISABLE, LAVISH_AXI_HOST, FM_TASK_ID, TRACEPARENT) through a new `spawn_prelaunch_export` collector that prepends them to the staged launch command, so the pane receives one text write instead of fusing separate `pane run` lines into a broken command; other pane backends still type each export as its own line.
- Skip Herdr's explicit `cd` into the recorded worktree when the pane shell already reports that path, leaving the pre-launch path read as the launch-boundary refusal, and keep the TRACEPARENT-rollback and env-allowlist behavior intact.
- Add `tests/fm-spawn-herdr-prelaunch-fusion.test.sh` (registered in `bin/fm-test-run.sh` and CI timings) covering ship/scout fresh spawn and relaunch as a single launch literal, and update `docs/agent-control.md`, `docs/herdr-backend.md`, and the trace-context docs and tests for the staged-launch carrier.

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: The behavior change is narrowly scoped to Herdr's pre-launch delivery, leaves every other backend's typing path identical, keeps trace rollback and allowlist ordering intact, and ships a regression test that fails on the old multi-write behavior; the only findings are documentation/comment precision.

## Testing

The Test agent exceeded its invocation budget before live validation completed; no evidence was gathered for this head.

'<file>'` does, see lines 152-163), so the check is now vacuous: a disabled remote spawn that wrongly exported a carrier into the staged launch file would pass it. The assertion is the only guard that a tracing-off spawn delivers no carrier to the remote pane (`remote_launch_snapshot` at line 190 only checks FM_TRACE_CONTEXT), so the regression it exists to catch is no longer detectable. Fix (same file, same block): assert on `remote_staged_launch` instead, e.g. `! remote_staged_launch | grep -q 'export TRACEPARENT='`, which keeps the independent oracle (the delivered launch text) while still failing on a leaked carrier.

🔧 Fix applied.
2 infos still open:

- ℹ️ `docs/herdr-backend.md:677` - The round-2 reword still claims "a spawn types its whole pre-launch as one text write", which is not true on a fresh Herdr spawn: `spawn_enter_recorded_worktree` types `cd -- <wt>` through `spawn_send_text_line` (bin/fm-spawn.sh:5589), i.e. a `pane run`, before the launch literal, and the drift-recovery path does the same (bin/fm-spawn.sh:6094). Only the export statements and the launch are now one write, and only an in-worktree relaunch is zero pre-launch runs (the line the fixer added next). Same overstatement in the sibling sentence at docs/trace-context.md:107 ("the carrier rides the one text write a spawn types"). Smallest remedy: say the exports and the launch are one write, and leave the relaunch claim to the following sentence.
- ℹ️ `bin/backends/herdr.sh:3224` - The reworded header comment now names only `treehouse get` as the spawn-time user of `fm_backend_herdr_send_text_line`, but Herdr never types that command: it takes the out-of-pane lease instead (bin/fm-spawn.sh:6113-6115), so the only texts this adapter carries for a spawn on this backend are the worktree-entry `cd --` (bin/fm-spawn.sh:5589) and the relaunch-recovery `cd --` (bin/fm-spawn.sh:6094). Fix the parenthetical to name `cd --` (the pre-launch worktree entry) so the comment matches its only real caller.

title: fix(watch): batch check-sweep wakes after the full alphabetical sweep
body:
## What Changed
- Batched check-sweep wakes in `bin/fm-watch.sh`: actionable check results (including merged-poll rows, rejected checks, park-on-review, and contribution output) are now queued via a new `queue_check_wake` helper and delivered in a single `wake` at the end of the alphabetical check sweep, instead of waking immediately per result — an early actionable check can no longer exit the watcher and starve later checks of their exact-once results.
- Extended tests to cover the batched sweep: a new `test_check_sweep_finishes_before_waking` case in `tests/fm-wake-queue.test.sh` verifies in both quiet and actionable modes that every registered check runs exactly once, results queue exactly once, and cadence advances; merged-poll cases in `tests/fm-pr-check-security.test.sh` now assert the complete sweep output (poll row plus later control-check result, in order) instead of only the first line.
- Aligned `bin/fm-merge-outcome-lib.sh` comments and `docs/architecture.md` with the new behavior: the poll's actionable row is delivered at the check sweep's end rather than immediately after outcome publication.

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: A small, focused batching of six wake sites into one end-of-sweep wake with an exact-once durable-append invariant preserved per row, the earlier fallthrough double-append/double-release bug already fixed by c0942c53, every stdout consumer (arm, checkpoint, guards, autoarm banner, supervision host, daemon) verified line-oriented and queue-backed, and native regression tests in both suites covering the quiet and actionable starvation modes plus ordered merged sweeps.

## Testing

Drove the changed watcher check sweep live four ways: the complete native tests/fm-wake-queue.test.sh suite (exit 0, includes the new durable regression proving an early actionable check cannot starve later alphabetical checks in quiet and actionable modes), the complete native tests/fm-pr-check-security.test.sh suite (exit 0, merged/degraded poll results cannot end the sweep early; trust/snapshot behavior preserved), two hand-driven real bin/fm-watch.sh cycles in disposable registered-check state dirs producing transcript artifacts (full a-early,m-middle,z-late sweep, one ordered end-of-sweep wake, exactly one durable drain record per result, .last-check advanced, exit 0), and an adversarial pre-fix reproduction against the base commit's watcher that failed exactly as the bug describes (sweep died at a-early). No UI surface is involved, so evidence is watcher transcripts and suite logs rather than screenshots. All disposable fixtures and the prefix tree were removed; the worktree is clean; no background work remains.

title: fix(bin): read the mail-check poll budget from the home .env
body:
## Intent

Identify and fix the mail check timeouts.

Context: overnight the mailbox poll check timed out twice, each time reporting that it ran out of its 15-second budget. This home's .env already sets FM_MAIL_CHECK_BUDGET=25, yet the timeouts name a 15-second budget. Manual mailbox reads against Gmail IMAP from this machine took 2s, 30s, and 3s, so Gmail is occasionally slow.

## What Changed

- `bin/fm-mail-check.sh` now sources `bin/fm-env-lib.sh` and fills `FM_MAIL_CHECK_BUDGET` from `$FM_HOME/.env` via `fmx_env_get` when the environment does not set it (environment still wins), so the watcher's shim — which never loads that file — stops polling on the default 15s budget when the home configures a larger one. Zero-padded spellings are stripped before the value is range-checked, and the budget is still cut down to fit `FM_CHECK_TIMEOUT`.
- An unparseable or out-of-range budget no longer exits 2 before the poll. The check falls back to the 15s default, keeps polling, and appends `FM_MAIL_CHECK_BUDGET=<value> is not a whole number from 5 to 25; polling on the <n>s budget` to its single stdout line after the poll's own finding, so the line cap trims the configuration note rather than the poll result; `arm` and `disarm` stay usable on such a home.
- Added `tests/fm-mail-check.test.sh` coverage for the `.env`/environment precedence, the watcher-bound clamp, padded values, and the rejected-budget fallback line; routed `bin/fm-env-lib.sh` changes to that test in `bin/fm-test-run.sh`, raised its CI timing estimate, and documented the new resolution and fallback behavior in `docs/configuration.md`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Risk Assessment

⚠️ Medium: The change correctly diagnoses and fixes the root cause (the watcher never loaded the home .env, so the budget was always 15) in a small, well-bounded way with a genuine regression test, but two concerns are worth addressing: an out-of-range .env value now silently disables the mail poll entirely because the watcher discards the check's stderr, and the intent's own 30s observation still exceeds the 25s ceiling this code can grant.

## Testing

I stood up throwaway FM_HOMEs with their own .env, state, bin and a fake python3, armed the real standing check, and let the real bin/fm-watch.sh dispatch the trust-bound state/mail.check.sh shim — the same path the overnight incident ran through. At base 68918448 the incident reproduces verbatim: a 20s poll in a home whose .env sets FM_MAIL_CHECK_BUDGET=25 wakes with the 15s-budget line and queues no mail; at HEAD the identical fixture completes the poll, emits "new mail: woke for 91", and leaves a durable mail wake row. Measuring wall clock against a never-returning poll confirms the budget is genuinely enforced at the value named (25s from .env, 5s when the environment overrides, 7s under FM_CHECK_TIMEOUT=10, 7s for the padded spelling 007). On the guard side, base exits 2 with nothing on the stdout the watcher consumes and refuses arm for an out-of-range value, while HEAD polls on the default, queues the mail, and carries the rejected value into the one wake line — including through a full watcher sweep for an annotated .env value — and arm/disarm stay usable; 4, 26, 000, abc and a 12-digit overflow value are all rejected without becoming the deadline, and 5, 25, 025 and 0000000005 are accepted. A 200-char annotated value leaves the poll's own "connection refused" finding intact and the cut lands on the trailing configuration note. The existing tests/fm-mail-check.test.sh suite passes in 25s, matching the refreshed CI timing hint, and the changed-test selector now picks that suite for an edit to bin/fm-env-lib.sh. The change is CLI/watcher-only with no rendered surface, so the evidence is CLI transcripts rather than screenshots. The disposable lab was removed and the worktree is clean.

title: fix(bin): keep relaunched Herdr workers in their own row with their own session
body:
## Problem

When a relaunch found the worker's Herdr pane gone, it re-created the tab in the workspace of the seat doing the reclaim.
The worker then showed as a second row under that seat's name.
A Claude relaunch in an adopted pane also started a fresh session while Herdr kept the old binding, so the sidebar showed the old session's idle time.

## Fix

- The reclaim now follows the same presentation rule as a fresh spawn: it joins the task's surviving bound projection workspace, or creates a fresh task-named projection when that workspace is gone, and only falls back to the flat container otherwise.
- The presentation probe is pinned to the recorded session.
- A Claude relaunch in an adopted pane moves the binding to a new session id with a clear report, and starts Claude with `--session-id` on that id.
- A relaunch test no longer uses GNU-only `sed -i` or depends on a real `pi` on PATH, and three smoke-test wait loops are widened because they flaked under load.

## Tests

- `tests/fm-backend-herdr.test.sh`, `tests/fm-control-herdr-smoke.test.sh`, `tests/fm-control-relaunch.test.sh`, and `tests/fm-control.test.sh` pass.
- `bin/fm-lint.sh` and `bin/fm-doc-audience-check.sh` pass.


Replaces #7898 (same fix, rebased onto current main).

title: fm-inbox note --request-id replay reports "saved, acknowledged" for a note it never wrote
body:
> [!NOTE]
> 🤖 **Claude Fable 5.2 responding on behalf of MDgoodlife**

`fm-inbox.sh note --request-id <rid>` on a retry whose request id is already reserved, but whose note was never published (the crash window the replay path exists for), can exit 0 with `"saved":true,"acknowledged":true` while no note exists anywhere.

Why: `publish_from_reservation` runs inside `id=$(publish_from_reservation ...) || die ...`, so errexit does not apply inside it. If `mktemp` for the staging file fails, `write_note_file ""` and `mv ""` both fail, and the function still prints the id and returns 0. `finish_note_result` then asks `announce_note`, which returns 2 ("acknowledged") because no pending file exists, and maps that to `acknowledged=1`.

Repro (main `427056c4`, scratch home; `publish_from_reservation` is unchanged on `68918448`):

1. create a reservation `state/inbox/.requests/rid-1` containing `1700000000-lost`, with no note for it;
2. put a `mktemp` shim on PATH that fails only for `.staging-` names;
3. `bin/fm-inbox.sh note --request-id rid-1 --json "x" </dev/null`

Got: exit 0, `{"outcome":"replay","id":"1700000000-lost","saved":true,"announced":false,"acknowledged":true,...}`; no pending note, no handled note, no wake.
Side effect of the same missing note: without `</dev/null` the call can hang, because the summary read ends up calling awk with an empty file name, which reads stdin.

Expected: exit 1 ("nothing saved"), the reservation kept, and a later retry with the same request id writes and announces the note once.

Fix that works locally: return 1 from each write step in `publish_from_reservation` (`mktemp ... || return 1`, and `write_note_file ... && mv ...` or `rm` the temp file and return 1). One function plus one case in `tests/fm-inbox.test.sh` (fails before, passes after). Happy to send it through no-mistakes if it fits.

title: Port of #6521: away-mode spend cap with whole-count startup budget
Port of #7390: per-secondmate Treehouse pool outside the home
body:
Speaking as Kun's firstmate: this is a port of #7390 by @FrankieShoe, opened from a branch on this repo.

Last-resort port of #7390

#7390 conflicts with main, and the resolved branch carries main's `.github/workflows/ci.yml` changes, which we can't push to a fork branch. So the resolved work lands here instead. All credit goes to @FrankieShoe.

What it does:
- Each local secondmate home gets its own Treehouse pool through a persistent `--root`. Return and park find the pool from the slot path.
- The per-secondmate pool root sits outside the firstmate home, at `${TREEHOUSE_ROOT:-$HOME/.treehouse}/fm-secondmate/<home-id>` (home-id is the `git hash-object` of the resolved home path). That keeps the home's `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` out of every slot's ancestors. A test walks every ancestor of a slot to check this.
- A relative `TREEHOUSE_ROOT` is ignored, and a root inside the home is refused (spawn fails closed).
- Secondmate-home teardown removes that home's pool root, as it did when the pool lived under the home.
- The bootstrap pool report scans those pools and leaves them out of the duplicate-clone check.
- The Treehouse installer pin moves from 2.0.1 to 2.3.0, with all four SHA256s.

The pin bump puts this under SKIPGATE-02: the captain merges it himself, no bot merge. It still needs a no-skip no-mistakes run and the Full suite.

title: A generic handled call on a worker-owned board's open round breaks the worker's next reply
body:
## Observed

A worker that hosts a Lavish review board owns it as a task-owned process-event source.
`docs/configuration.md` ("Crew-hosted Lavish review boards", on `68918448`) says a captured nonterminal round stays open until the worker re-arms, and the re-arm both posts the reply and acknowledges that round.
It reserves `bin/fm-procevent.sh handled <source-id> <sequence>` for concluding a terminal round.

The code does not enforce that split.
`cmd_handled` (`bin/fm-procevent.sh` lines 2116-2167) checks whether a task-owned capture is terminal only to decide whether to retire the board.
For a nonterminal capture it still calls `fm_procevent_mark_handled` and prints `handled: <id> <seq>`.

`cmd_register_task` (lines 556-690) then refuses the worker's re-arm, because the source is already registered to that task and no unacknowledged round is left.
The refusal is `cannot re-arm source <id>: task <task> already holds this board and no captured round is waiting to be acknowledged`.
Because a refused arm never posts the reply, the worker's ordinary reply step fails.

## Expected

`handled` refuses a task-owned nonterminal capture before it writes any acknowledgement, and names the worker's re-arm as the step that acknowledges that round.
These keep working as today:

- `handled` on a task-owned terminal round concludes and retires the board.
- A repeated `handled` on that terminal round prints `already-handled`.
- `handled` on any source that is not task-owned behaves as today.

Reply delivery and nonterminal acknowledgement stay in the worker's re-arm.

## Consequence

In one fleet, a captain submitted board feedback.
The worker had read it in full 14 seconds later and started on it.
A supervisor then wrongly concluded the feedback was unread, sent it to the worker again and ran `handled` on the open round.
About three minutes later the worker's reply-and-re-arm was refused with the message above.
The reply reached the board only after the worker fell back to the adapter's direct reply command, 30 seconds after the refusal.

## How to verify

1. Have a worker arm a task-owned Lavish board and let a nonterminal feedback round be captured.
2. Run `bin/fm-procevent.sh handled <source-id> <sequence>` for that round as the supervisor.
3. Check that the call is refused, and that it records no acknowledgement.
4. Check that the worker's re-arm with `--agent-reply-file` then posts the reply and acknowledges the round.
5. Check that `handled` on a terminal round of the same board still concludes it, and that a repeated call prints `already-handled`.

Related: https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/issues/7280 (open) covers the stuck-busy alert that can prompt such an intervention, not the acknowledgement itself.

title: fix(bin): treat a watcher beacon stamped ahead of the clock as fresh
body:
## Intent Speaking as mikeastwoody's firstmate: approved contribution to #8426, chosen from a shortlist of ready-for-pr issues. Substance of the approved issue: `bin/fm-guard.sh` prints the full "WATCHER DOWN - SUPERVISION IS OFF" banner while the watcher is healthy whenever the liveness beacon's mtime is one or two seconds ahead of the guard's clock read; the banner itself shows "last beat: -2s ago". `fm_path_age` in `bin/fm-wake-lib.sh` returns `now - mtime`, so such a beacon gives a negative age, and `fm_watcher_supervision_verdict` runs that age through a `''|*[!0-9]*)` digit test that treats `-1` or `-2` as not a number and leaves the beacon not fresh. A beacon stamped slightly ahead of the clock is fresh, as the strict check `fm_watcher_healthy` already treats it: clamp a negative age to zero before the digit test, and add a guard fixture test with the beacon mtime at `now + 2` that must not print the banner. Contract class (maintainer triage): restore. ## What Changed - `fm_watcher_supervision_verdict` in `bin/fm-wake-lib.sh` now sets a negative beacon age to zero before its digit check. A `.last-watcher-beat` whose mtime is slightly ahead of the guard's clock now counts as fresh, which matches `fm_watcher_healthy`. Before this change, such a beacon failed the check as "not a number" and `fm-guard.sh` printed the "WATCHER DOWN" banner with a negative "last beat" age. - Added `test_autoarm_future_beacon_is_fresh_not_a_banner` to `tests/fm-guard-stale-banner.test.sh`. It sets the beacon mtime to now + 2s and asserts that the auto-arm guard prints nothing. - Updated the coverage list in `docs/turnend-guard.md` to include the future-stamped beacon case. ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: The change is a two-line clamp that only affects a negative age, which only a beacon stamped ahead of the clock can produce. It matches how `fm_watcher_healthy` already treats that case. The new test runs `fm-guard.sh` and asserts the issue's stated behaviour, and it would have failed before the fix. ## Testing I ran the real fm-guard.sh against disposable lab homes made with fm-lab-home.sh, at the target commit and at the base commit. With the beacon 1–2 s ahead of the clock, the base guard printed the full WATCHER DOWN banner ("last beat: -1s ago"). The fixed guard printed nothing. As adversarial checks, a beacon at 0 s stayed silent, and a 600 s-old beacon and a missing beacon still raised the banner with the right reason. I ran the new fixture test on its own in throwaway copies: it passes with the fix and fails with the base library, reproducing the reported "-2s ago" banner. title: feat(bin): show captain deferral dates on OPEN DECISIONS drain rows
body:
## Intent

Speaking as mikeastwoody's firstmate: approved contribution to #8436, chosen from a shortlist of ready-for-pr issues.

Substance of the approved issue: the `OPEN DECISIONS` section of `bin/fm-wake-drain.sh` re-presents a captain decision on every drain with no sign that the captain already deferred it to a date. `bin/fm-captain-hold.sh hold --until YYYY-MM-DD` records a `[until=YYYY-MM-DD]` field, and the open-decision reminders already honor it, but the drain builds its listing from the untimed projection of the status-log fold (`scan_open_decisions_incremental`, which calls `status_open_decisions_incremental` without the `timed` view), so each row is only task, key, verb and note and the date is dropped. The fold already computes the deferral column in its `timed` view. Wanted: when a deferral is current, the drain row shows its date, for example `<task> [key=<key>] [until=2026-12-11] needs-decision: <note>`, so a reader can tell a deferred call from one owed now; deferred calls stay listed. Keep the newest-line-wins rule (a later undated republish clears the date), keep the reminder schedule untouched, keep the existing per-line cap, and add a status-log fixture test showing that an `[until=]` status line produces a drain row with the same date. Contract class (maintainer triage): new-default.

Speaking as mikeastwoody's firstmate: follow-up requested by the maintainer after the labelled full run on the first head found a regression. Once the drain reads the timed fold, the self-announced `--resolve-key` check must keep working: `fm_wake_status_append_self_announced` in `bin/fm-wake-lib.sh` accepts a close after a drain-presented decision as this home's own bookkeeping only when the untimed fold cursor already sits at the pre-append size, so the drain must advance the untimed cursor too, not only the timed one. Keep the #4767 test (`test_multiple_keys_close_after_fold_is_self_announced` in `tests/fm-send-resolve-key.test.sh`) passing as is, and add coverage for an `[until=]` row with a close after it, which must be self-announced and must not re-wake the home. Current upstream main is merged into the branch (merge, not rebase).

## What Changed
- `bin/fm-wake-drain.sh`'s OPEN DECISIONS section now builds its rows from the fold's timed view. When the newest line for a key carries a valid `[until=YYYY-MM-DD]` date, the row includes it, e.g. `<task> [key=<key>] [until=2026-12-11] needs-decision: <note>`. Deferred decisions stay listed. A later undated republish clears the date because the newest line wins. The per-line and total byte caps are unchanged.
- The drain still advances the untimed fold cursor before it reads the timed view. This keeps `fm_wake_status_append_self_announced` treating a `--resolve-key` close after a listed decision as this home's own bookkeeping. To support this, `scan_open_decisions_incremental` and `scan_open_decisions_snapshot` in `bin/fm-classify-lib.sh` accept an optional `timed` argument. Comments in `bin/fm-watch.sh` and the `.open-decisions-cursor` entry in the operational-home-layout skill now describe the `.timed` cursor that the drain and reminders share.
- Two tests are new. One is a status-log fixture: an `[until=]` line gives a drain row with the same date, an undated row keeps its shape, and an undated republish clears the date. The other checks that closing a deferred key with `--resolve-key` after a drain does not wake the home again. The cursor tests now point at the `.timed` cursor file.

## Risk Assessment

✅ Low: The drain now renders rows from the fold's existing timed view and still advances the untimed cursor in both the snapshot and non-snapshot paths. The open/closed rules, the per-line cap, the reminder schedule and teardown cleanup (which already removes the `.timed` cursor) are unchanged, and the one cost is a second bounded incremental fold per drain.

## Testing

I ran the real hold → parent channel → drain → `fm-send --resolve-key` path in a throwaway lab: a parent lab home, a local secondmate home, and a private `fm-lab` tmux socket. Each step was recorded as a transcript. The drain rows showed the deferral date, re-dated holds took the new date, and an undated republish cleared it. Malformed dates were left off and long notes were still capped at the 220-byte line limit (row measured at 219 bytes). On the current head, answering a deferred decision after a drain was self-announced and did not re-wake the home. The same flow with the first head's scripts reproduced the reported re-wake regression. The four targeted test files passed, covering the drain, its cursors, `--resolve-key` (including the #4767 test, unchanged) and the reminder schedule. Overall result: go. The lab, its tmux server and temp files were removed; the worktree is clean. This is CLI-only, so there are no screenshots.

title: fm-crew-state reports a launch that never started its brief as working, with no time limit
body:
## Observed

`bin/fm-spawn.sh` seeds each worker's busy record as `state=busy source=fm-spawn`, and the worker's hooks advance it once the worker starts its brief.
`bin/fm-busy-lib.sh` (classification rule 4, lines 74-86 on `68918448`) keeps an untouched seed as busy.
The only exception is when the captured pane shows a recognized trust, sign-in or first-run prompt.
`bin/fm-crew-state.sh` (line 1612) then prints `state: working · source: pane · harness busy (fm-spawn)`.

The one-hour bound `BUSY_TURN_MAX_SECS` drives only the watcher's alerts.
It does not change what `fm-crew-state.sh` prints.
So a launch that died after the seed was written, and before the worker ever ran, reads as working for as long as the record exists.

## Expected

An untouched `source=fm-spawn` seed older than `BUSY_TURN_MAX_SECS` reads `unknown` with the reason "launch never confirmed", not `working`.
A seed that any hook event has advanced keeps today's verdict, however old the turn is.

## Consequence

In one fleet, a scheduled scout launch was very probably cut off after its task record and busy seed were written, and before the worker started.
The busy record still held the untouched seed nine hours later, and no session for that worker existed.
One hour after the launch, a waiting-too-long alert fired, and the supervisor called it transient because the state read working.
Nine hours after the launch, the state still read `working · harness busy (fm-spawn)`.
The scout's report was never produced.

## How to verify

1. Seed a task's busy record as `state=busy source=fm-spawn` with a timestamp one hour and one second old, and post no hook event.
2. Run `bin/fm-crew-state.sh <task>` and check that it prints `unknown` with "launch never confirmed".
3. Advance the same record with any hook event and check that it reads `working` again.

Related: https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/pull/8051 (open) adds a one-time watcher wake for a worker that has not started its brief about two minutes after spawn.
It does not change what the state reader prints, which supervision uses to judge later alerts.

title: A declared wait without an until time is rechecked only after four hours, so a forgotten wait stalls unseen
body:
## Observed

A worker declares a wait with a `paused:` status line.
The generated brief (`bin/fm-brief.sh` line 188 on `68918448`) asks for `until <YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MMZ>` only "when you know when the wait clears".
`bin/fm-classify-lib.sh` rechecks a declared wait at its `until` time, or else every `FM_PAUSE_RESURFACE_SECS` (default 14400, four hours).
The opt-in `config/pause-ceiling` turns an undated pause into a decision only after `FM_PAUSE_UNDATED_MAX_SECS` (default 86400, one day).

A wait on a draft PR's checks has no other monitor.
`bin/fm-pr-check.sh` refuses a draft PR and arms nothing, as its header says.
So a worker that declares an undated wait on a draft PR's CI, and then does not run its blocking wait, is not noticed for up to four hours.

## Expected

Every `paused:` line names an `until` time.
For CI, that is the expected finish plus some slack.
The brief asks for it on every declared wait, and a `paused:` line without one is not accepted as a declared wait.
A wait that names its time keeps today's behavior: it is rechecked at that time or at the four-hour cadence, whichever comes first.

## Consequence

In one fleet, a worker pushed a draft PR and declared `paused: ... Waiting on CI` with no time.
It ran no blocking check wait and ended its turn.
It sat idle for 3 hours 31 minutes, until the captain asked why the PR was still a draft.
Another PR that waited on it stalled for the same time.
With an `until` time of the CI duration plus slack, the recheck would have come well within the first hour.

## How to verify

1. Have a worker append `paused [at=<now>]: waiting on CI` with no `until`, then stop.
2. Check that the line is refused or surfaced at once as needing a time, not left for the four-hour recheck.
3. Append `paused [at=<now>]: waiting on CI until <now + 30 minutes>` and check that it is rechecked at that time.
4. Check that the generated brief asks for `until` on every declared wait.

Related: https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/issues/8692 (open) covers the other side: a wait known to last days is still rechecked every four hours.

title: gh-axi: reviews read fails on builds where `gh api` has no `--slurp`
body:
## What happened

`gh-axi pr view <n> --reviews` fails outright with `unknown flag: --slurp`. The same failure hits the contributions observer's inline read, so on this machine every owned GitHub pull request stays permanently unmeasured, and it also took out the pipeline's CI check-read during a delivery (its gate escalated the identical error and could only be closed by hand).

## Machine facts

- `gh version 2.46.0 (2025-12-13 Ubuntu 2.46.0-4)`
- `gh api <endpoint> --slurp` → `unknown flag: --slurp`, and the flag list gh prints for `gh api` on this build has no `--slurp`.
- The same endpoint called plainly returns normally: reviews for the tested pull request came back as an empty list with no error.
- So the wrapper is the failing part, not authentication, not the network, not the repository.

## Smallest fix

Ask the endpoint plainly and wrap the response into an array (the query layer already does this), or probe whether the installed `gh` accepts the flag before adding it. Either way the read should degrade to the plain call instead of failing the whole observation.

## Impact on a fleet run this way

- Contribution observation for GitHub pull requests can never complete, so a reviewer comment on a fleet-owned pull request would go unnoticed here.
- Any delivery run on a repository with real checks would trip the same read and escalate a decision that a human has to answer by hand every time.

## Repro

1. On a machine where `gh api <endpoint> --slurp` errors, run `gh-axi pr view <n> --reviews`.
2. Run the same endpoint without the flag: it answers correctly.

title: Claude primary: the default-on supervision host is invisible to the operator and reads as firstmate delegating to itself
body:
On a Claude primary the supervision host is on by default (`docs/configuration.md`, "Supervision host"). Nothing announces it, so an operator watching their terminal multiplexer sees a second, headless firstmate session working: handling wakes, dispatching from an away queue and cleaning up merged lanes, while the main session sits idle. In one home the operator read this as the primary breaking the "supervise, don't do the work" contract and stopped the session to ask why.

### Expected

The operator can tell from the primary's own output when the host has acted and why, for example:
- one line in the primary's next turn: "the supervision host handled N wakes: ...";
- a startup line that explains what the host is, not only "Supervision host: on".

### Notes

The opt-out file exists. The problem is not the default itself but that it is invisible, and that its account of what it did does not reliably come back to the primary. Related: #7485, #8671.

title: fm-contributions.sh: a check-runs 403 on a fine-grained token discards the entire observation
body:
### Summary

`bin/fm-contributions.sh poll` treats a `403` on the check-runs read as a failure
of the whole observation. Because the check-runs permission cannot be granted to
a fine-grained personal access token at all, any home authenticating with one
never produces a usable contributions observation — including the comment and
review signals it *can* read perfectly well.

The practical effect is that PR comment and review notification silently never
works on a fine-grained token, even though five of the six underlying reads
succeed.

### Environment

- firstmate at commit `427056c4` (current main at time of writing; still present)
- `gh` 2.102.0 (installed from the upstream `cli/cli` release)
- GitHub.com, authenticated with a **fine-grained** personal access token
  holding repository read permissions including Contents, Pull requests,
  Commit statuses and Actions

### What happens

With the token above, the six reads one PR observation performs resolve as:

| Read | Endpoint | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PR comments | `repos/{r}/issues/{n}/comments` | 200 |
| PR reviews | `repos/{r}/pulls/{n}/reviews` | 200 |
| Inline review comments | `repos/{r}/pulls/{n}/comments` | 200 |
| Commit statuses | `repos/{r}/commits/{sha}/statuses` | 200 |
| Workflow runs | `repos/{r}/actions/runs` | 200 |
| Check runs | `repos/{r}/commits/{sha}/check-runs` | **403 Resource not accessible by personal access token** |

The record then stores:

```
error: forge observation unavailable: checks read exited 1 with 18s of budget
       left: gh: Resource not accessible by personal access token (HTTP 403)
observation: null
```

`fm-contributions.sh pending` returns `[]`, which is indistinguishable from
"nothing needs attention" for a caller that does not inspect `error`.

### Why a token permission cannot fix it

The "Checks" repository permission is not offered for fine-grained personal
access tokens; it is available to GitHub Apps only. So unlike the commit-statuses
and Actions reads — which a user can grant and which then succeed — this gap is
not closeable by configuring the token. Any fine-grained-token home is affected
permanently.

A classic token with `repo` scope is a workaround, but asking users to downgrade
to a broader, less granular credential to regain comment notifications is the
wrong trade.

### Proposed fix

Treat an authorization failure on the check-runs read as a **declared coverage
limit** rather than a failed observation, reusing the distinction the tool
already draws for a deliberately small budget ("remains bounded and may be
unmeasured, rather than being mislabeled unavailable"):

1. On `403`/`404` from the check-runs read specifically, do not null the
   observation. Build it from the reads that succeeded and mark check coverage
   `unmeasured` with the reason.
2. Keep comment, review, inline-comment, status and workflow-run signals fully
   live, so PR feedback notification works on a fine-grained token.
3. Keep genuine failures unchanged — a transient error, a rate limit, or an
   authorization failure on any *other* read should still record
   `observation unavailable` as today.
4. Surface the reduced coverage honestly wherever coverage is reported, so a
   caller never reads partial check coverage as proven-clear.

This keeps the existing "a failed read is not silence" guarantee intact while
not letting one structurally ungrantable permission erase five working signals.

### Notes

- Not a regression; it appears to have been the behavior since the coherent
  single-observation model was introduced.
- Happy to supply a patch if the maintainers agree with the direction.

title: persistent-cd guard: ~1 denial per session from `cd <dir> && cmd`; consider rewriting into a subshell
body:
In one Claude primary home over six weeks, the persistent-cd guard denied 100 commands across about 170 sessions, at a steady rate after #6502 and #7995 were fixed. Almost all were `cd <project-or-tmp> && <read-only command>`. Each denial costs a model turn and a retry, and the retry is always the same command wrapped as `( cd X && ... )` or rewritten with `git -C`.

### Proposal

Claude Code's PreToolUse hook can return `updatedInput`. For the safe shape (a leading `cd <dir> &&` with no later top-level `cd`), the guard could wrap the command in a subshell and allow it, keeping the deny for anything else. Unverified whether the other harness adapters can rewrite input; the deny could stay the fallback there.

title: fm-usage-warner.sh refuses to arm on Linux/WSL (osascript-only notifier)
body:
`bin/fm-usage-warner.sh` arms only on Darwin and notifies only through `osascript`. On Linux/WSL it prints "Notification Center is only available on macOS; nothing to arm". The threshold logic itself works on any platform; one home now runs a custom watcher check that calls `fm-usage-warner.sh check` and relays crossings through the normal wake.

### Proposal

When `osascript` is missing, deliver the crossing as a fleet wake (or via `notify-send` if present) instead of refusing. Related: #106 (pluggable notifier).

title: fm-bootstrap.sh does not check the gh version, but fm-contributions.sh needs gh api --slurp
body:
Bootstrap checks that `gh` exists (`COMMON_TOOLS`) but not its version. Distribution packages can ship a `gh` without `gh api --slurp`. With such a version, `bin/fm-contributions.sh` (which uses `--paginate --slurp`) fails every poll and PR monitoring silently stops; in one home this went unnoticed until a newer `gh` was installed by hand.

### Proposal

An `OUTDATED: gh` bootstrap line with a minimum version, like the existing `gh-axi` check. The exact minimum is unverified; `--slurp` appears to have arrived around gh 2.48.

title: fix(bin): let inbox records inherit a folder's default ACL
body:
## Intent A steering record must be readable by every account the inbox folder's permissions allow. Today the inbox writer creates its staging file with mktemp, which forces mode 600, and renames it into place. On a folder with a default POSIX ACL that grants a second account read access, mode 600 sets the new file's ACL mask to empty, so the second account's entry is in the list but has no effect and the record cannot be read. Fix it so a new record gets the mode an ordinary file created in that folder would get, and the inherited ACL entry is effective. Nothing else about the record's writing (atomic rename, locking, ordering) changes. ## What Changed - `bin/fm-task-inbox-lib.sh`: the inbox writer no longer creates its staging file with `mktemp`, whose fixed mode 600 emptied the ACL mask inherited from a folder's default ACL. It now picks a name with `mktemp -u` and creates it exclusively (`set -C`) under `umask 077`. A plain folder still gets mode 600, and a folder with a default ACL decides the mode, so its named entries stay effective. The atomic rename, locking and ordering are unchanged. - `tests/fm-task-inbox.test.sh`: two new tests. One checks that a record stays `-rw-------` in a folder without a default ACL under umask 022 and 077. The other checks that a record's ACL matches the ACL of an ordinary file created in a folder with a default ACL. It skips when the system has no POSIX ACL support. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) ## Risk Assessment ✅ Low: A one-line change to how the staging file is created. It keeps exclusive creation (noclobber uses O_EXCL and does not follow symlinks), the lock, the atomic rename and the cleanup. The only open question is the intended mode in folders without a default ACL. ## Testing I drove the real inbox writer from the base commit and from the fix on disposable tmpfs folders with a default POSIX ACL. Base: records were 600 with mask::--- and the named entry showed #effective:---, which reproduces the bug. Fix: records matched an ordinary file exactly (mask::r--, named entry #effective:r--) under both umask 077 and 022. With no ACL, records stay 600, which matches the recorded decision. Bodies read back intact and no staging files were left. The targeted inbox test file passed, including the concurrent-writer and sequence tests. The sandbox's user namespace maps only the worker uid, so the setfacl entry used that uid. The kernel rejected uid 1000 with EINVAL, so a real read by a second account was not exercised. The mask computation is the same for any named entry. - Live validation: ✅ go - 4 of 5 scenarios driven live against the product | Scenario | Result | Live | Evidence | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Base commit reproduces the bug: in a default-ACL folder (user:<uid>:r) the record gets mask::--- and the named entry has no effect | ✅ pass | live | acl-record-modes.txt, BASE section: 001.msg/002.msg show `user:<uid>:r-- #effective:---`, `mask::---`; the ordinary file shows `#effective:r--` | | Fix: a record in a default-ACL folder gets the same ACL and mode as an ordinary file, with the inherited entry effective (umask 077 and 022) | ✅ pass | live | acl-record-modes.txt, FIX sections: records are -rw-r--r--+ with `mask::r--` and `user:<uid>:r-- #effective:r--`, identical to `ordinary` | | A record in a plain folder with no default ACL stays mode 600 under umask 022 (behaviour kept by the declined review decision) | ✅ pass | live | acl-record-modes.txt, last section: records are -rw------- while the ordinary file is -rw-r--r-- | | Writing is otherwise unchanged: sequence order, readback, no leftover staging files, concurrent writers lose nothing | ✅ pass | live | acl-record-modes.txt (001/002 ordered, body readback, 0 staging files); fm-task-inbox-test.txt 'concurrent writers serialize on the sequence lock and lose nothing' | | A real second account (uid 1000) can open the record | ⏸️ untested | no | The sandbox's user namespace maps only the worker uid, so the kernel rejects an entry for uid 1000, and switching accounts needs sudo, which is not allowed. To cover this, run the same script on the h… |

title: Port of #6870: exclude omp daemon workers from session lock anchoring
body:
Speaking as Kun's firstmate: this is a last-resort port of #6870 by @avivl, opened from a branch on this repo because #6870 has been conflicting with main since #6300. Thank you @avivl for the fix; your commit is kept with your authorship.

Last-resort port of #6870

## What it does
An omp daemon worker (`__omp_worker_*`) is never recorded as the session-lock anchor. A lock pinned to one reads as stale, and `fm-lock.sh` refuses under an omp daemon worker with a named error. Relates to #8089.

## Conflict resolution
Main's newer behavior is kept, and the exclusion is added on top:
- `fm_proc_info` in the ancestry walk (not raw `ps`)
- main's Windows lock-error path
- `agy` in `FM_HARNESS_RE`
- main's `fm_omp_process_matches` wording in the harness docs

Commits from #6870 that are already on main, or empty on this tree, were dropped (`fd13ce62`, `65e058aa`, `4cac953b`).

## Caveats
- **Vendor contract:** the exclusion relies on omp's internal `__omp_worker_*` argv token, which has been verified only on omp 18.8.x. If a later omp rewrites the process args (for example via `setProcessName`), the worker would read as an omp harness again.
- **Known follow-up, kept out of scope:** bun-installed omp spawns workers as `bun .../cli.js __omp_worker_*`, and `fm_omp_daemon_worker` checks only the first argument, so that shape isn't excluded yet. This port keeps #6870's scope. Filed as #8777.

## Checks
- Local: session-lock ancestry 32/32 (including the 2 new omp-worker cases), ps-denied, windows-consumers 3/3, omp-harness 21/21, lint and the doc audience check all pass.
- Adversarial review: low risk, no errors.
- Contract class: restore.
- Full suite 45512013486 green on head 5946ec25. Merged as dbb3f19679e83bae0259b1424d96da99a9ea2578.

title: tests/fm-park.test.sh pending-hang test fails under a non-C locale because lane files sort differently
body:
## Observed

On `68918448`, `test_hung_pending_check_ends_within_the_tick` in `tests/fm-park.test.sh` fails with `not ok - pending-hang: the tick did not save the lane it never reached` when the shell locale is `en_US.UTF-8`.
It passes under `LC_ALL=C`.
It failed 3 of 3 runs under the default locale and passed 3 of 3 under `LC_ALL=C`.

## Cause

`cmd_tick` in `bin/fm-park.sh` builds its lane list from the glob `"$STATE"/*.review-park`, and bash sorts glob results by the current collation.
The test creates lanes `lane` and `lane2` and expects the tick, which runs out of time on the first lane, to save `lane2` in `.review-park-tick-next`.
Under C collation `lane.review-park` sorts before `lane2.review-park`, because `.` sorts before `2`.
Under `en_US.UTF-8` punctuation is ignored at the first level, so the order is `lane2 lane` and the tick correctly saves `lane`.
An xtrace run shows `visit_lanes ... watch_parked lane2 lane`.

The product code is fine: the cursor works for any lane order.
Only the test assumes C ordering, which is why CI in the C locale stays green.

## Expected

The test passes under any locale.
Either pin `LC_ALL=C` for the tick in this test, or use lane names whose order does not depend on collation, such as `lane-a` and `lane-b`.

## How to verify

1. Run `LANG=en_US.UTF-8 LC_ALL= bash tests/fm-park.test.sh` and see the pending-hang failure today.
2. Apply the fix and run it again under both `en_US.UTF-8` and `LC_ALL=C`; both pass.

Related: https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate/pull/7391 (open) fixes a different collation-dependent test failure in `bin/fm-test-run.sh`.
